statement: After storage, query and the high-level serving infrastructure, the remaining big piece of the word-dictionary design is seamless updates.
case_study: Word dictionary on S3: applying the weekly Oxford changelog to the one-file dictionary served by the API servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now this is still not done. There is still a big chunk remaining. Updates.

statement: Updates are weekly: every week Oxford sends a file containing only the words that changed and their new meanings (e.g. apple, ball and zoo changed), and these changes must be applied to the dictionary file on S3.
detail: Asked whether the whole dictionary or only the changelog arrives, the teacher answers: only the changelog.
case_study: Word dictionary on S3: applying the weekly Oxford changelog to the one-file dictionary served by the API servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: every week I'll get a file from Oxford which has the words that have changed and the new meaning for that.

statement: A student proposes a periodic (cron) job, triggered whenever an Oxford update arrives, that updates the dictionary and its index, repackages the whole file and uploads it to S3, running on a separate machine.
detail: The teacher accepts the idea of spinning up another server ("Now we are talking." / "You're spinning up another server.").
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: it will update the index, and so it will repackage the whole file, upload it to the S3
flags: check: "where ... it would update what?" may be the teacher probing
check: speaker of "Now we are talking." (Teacher?)

statement: The teacher distinguishes the terms: a batch job is batch processing, while what is needed here is a job doing periodic updates (a cron job).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: See, batch job is batch processing. Job is periodic updates.
flags: check: a word before "job" may be missing (cron?)

statement: The update job runs on a newly spun-up server that holds the changelog and downloads the current dictionary from S3.
case_study: Word dictionary on S3: applying the weekly Oxford changelog to the one-file dictionary served by the API servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Correct. You'll download it from S3.

statement: Bumping the version stored in the file header is the last step of the update; the real question is how the dictionary file itself gets updated.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: That's okay. That's the last thing that we'll do. But how are you updating the dictionary?

statement: A student proposes appending the changelog entries at the end of the dictionary, since the dictionary is not sorted.
detail: Teacher's correction: the dictionary would be ever increasing and contain duplicate entries, and the dictionary being served cannot have repetitive entries.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: the dictionary would be ever increasing, plus it would have duplicate entries.

statement: A student proposes iterating the whole dictionary once and, where a changelog word's meaning changed, replacing that entry.
detail: The teacher pushes back that it is not that simple and asks the student to go into more detail; the in-place replacement problem follows.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Is it really that simple? Think of it. Think, go into a little more details of it.

statement: Comparing hashes of the existing and new entries (or generating a diff) is unnecessary, because the changelog already states exactly what needs to change.
detail: Two student ideas corrected here: compare a hash of existing vs new (01:08:46) and "generate the diff" (01:09:27); the teacher: "Why do you want to generate a diff? Changelog already has this".
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Hash, you don't need it, because changelog directly contains the changes

statement: It is easy to build complex systems and very difficult to build simple ones; think about only the things you really need.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: as I always say, it's easy to build complex systems. It's very difficult to build simple systems.

statement: A student proposes using the in-memory index to find the offset of a changed word (e.g. apple) and replacing that whole CSV line in place in the dictionary file.
detail: The teacher then shows why this fails on disk: the longer meaning overwrites the following entry.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So we can use that index file and use the index and apply those changes or replace that the whole line of the CSV.

statement: Example: the file holds 'apple, a fruit' followed by 'ball, a round object'; the changelog says apple's new meaning is 'a round fruit'. Writing it at apple's offset (found via the index) raises the question whether the next entry moves down.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You say that using index, let's say you know the offset when it needs to be changed.
flags: check: start of "...by this? Yes." may be missing or a student's answer

statement: Limitation of how a disk works: when you go to a location in a file and start writing, the bytes are written blindly over whatever is there, so a longer replacement overwrites the next entry instead of shifting it down.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So when you go to a particular location and start writing, it would blindfoldedly write the bytes.
flags: check: "We have to do that happen in file IO." may be a student

statement: In an IDE you can hit enter and the other lines move down because the text is in memory; on disk you cannot do that.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Like in the IDE, when we add, we can hit enter and move other lines down. Because it is in memory.

statement: Therefore you cannot simply say 'I will replace the entry' in the file: writing apple's new meaning at its offset overrides the existing data.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You are overriding the existing one. So you cannot just say I would replace it because it's not as trivial.

statement: Focus on implementation details: it is easy to say 'I would replace it', but imagining the code you would write reveals the things that would break; this is what makes better engineers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: imagine you are the one implementing it. What code will you write to implement it?
flags: check: "Thanks, but thanks for making this." phrase after a 14 s pause, may be garbled

statement: A good or senior engineer always wears three hats: product manager, architect and engineer; thinking through the implementation is the engineer hat.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: An engineer, a good engineer or a senior engineer always wear three hats. Product manager, architect, and an engineer.

statement: A student proposes graveyard entries: append the new meaning at the end, waste the old entry's space for a while and later run a compaction process; the teacher rejects it: no repetitive entries are allowed, and since updates are only weekly the file should be cleaned up directly.
detail: Teacher: "No repetitive entries." and "we don't see it would work well when you are doing live updates. This is an even weekly update. So have it very clean up it directly."
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: I was thinking like you just sort of waste, waste that space for some time and later run some sort of compaction process after.

statement: A student proposes (calling it naive) creating a new file: find the byte where the change belongs, write the change into the new file, then append all the rest of the old file.
topic: dictionary > updates > merge into new file
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: we are creating a new file. Now, add that change in that file. And then append all the rest file to it.

statement: Creating a new file this way is not naive: it is like the merge step of merge sort, and given this design it is the best approach.
topic: dictionary > updates > merge into new file
speaker: teacher
verbatim: No, no, it's not naive, it's not naive, it's kind of like merge of merge sort, correct?

statement: The design deliberately avoids fancy structures like B+ trees: think of a simple approach and it will be really efficient; making things complex brings its own set of disadvantages.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We're not using fancy B+ trees over here, we're going with very simple approach

statement: For the merge-sort-style merge to be efficient, the dictionary file needs to be sorted.
topic: dictionary > updates > merge into new file
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the requirement to do that merge of merge sort, to be to be efficient, is that your file needs to be sorted.

statement: The update creates a new dictionary file by merging two files: the existing (sorted) dictionary downloaded onto the newly spun-up server and the changelog.
topic: dictionary > updates > merge into new file
case_study: Word dictionary on S3: applying the weekly Oxford changelog to the one-file dictionary served by the API servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So what we'll do is we'll create a new file out of the existing file. How? By merging the two files.

statement: The changelog is a very short file; if it is not sorted, load it in memory, sort it and dump it, since it is small.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Even if it is not sorted, you load it in memory, sort it and dump it, because it's going to be very small.

statement: The merge is the classic problem of merging two sorted linked lists / two sorted arrays into a third new sorted array (the merge step of merge sort).
topic: dictionary > updates > merge into new file
speaker: teacher
verbatim: merge two sorted linked list into third sorted, sorry, merge two sorted arrays into third new sorted array. This is that.

statement: Merge procedure: keep one pointer in each file and iterate both line by line; write the entry with the smaller word to the new file and advance that pointer; when the words match, write the changelog's updated meaning and advance both pointers.
topic: dictionary > updates > merge into new file
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you have a pointer over here, you have a pointer over here. You iterate both files line by line.

statement: Walkthrough: dictionary A A', B B', C C', D D', F F' merged with changelog C C'', E E', F F'': output A A', B B', C C'' (updated), D D', E E', F F'' (updated meaning picked); once the changelog is exhausted, every remaining dictionary entry follows.
detail: Letters stand for words and primed letters for meanings (a simplification). The changelog entry E E' has no match in the dictionary and is written in order.
topic: dictionary > updates > merge into new file
speaker: teacher
verbatim: CC dash, CC double dash. This is the updated one. Both matches.

statement: Unlike merging sorted arrays, the merge does not load the file into memory: it iterates the files line by line and writes a third file.
topic: dictionary > updates > merge into new file
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You are literally iterating file line by line and creating a third file out of it.

statement: Because file IO may override the next line if a write goes beyond its range, always create new entries (in a new file) rather than writing in place.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You have to always ensure that you are creating new entries over there.

statement: The dictionary is one terabyte, so the merged new file is also about one terabyte; the disk of the server spun up to run the update job must be at least two terabytes (acceptable, since it is just one server).
case_study: Word dictionary on S3: applying the weekly Oxford changelog to the one-file dictionary served by the API servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The disk of that server that we just spin up to run this job should be at least two terabyte, at least two terabyte, right?

statement: The merged file is a complete new dictionary: it also has its headers and index, all sorted, and is ready to upload to S3.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we also have headers, headers, index, all sorted for this file. So this is the new dictionary that we are ready to upload to S3.

statement: A student proposes uploading the new file to a new S3 path (new URL) and telling the clients/API servers to swap to it, i.e. 'change the pointer', while worrying about downtime during the switch.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: we have to tell the clients who are using this thing that we have a new file from where they have to read it.

statement: The same student frames switching API servers to the new file as a deployment problem: change everything in one go, a rolling upgrade, or a canary where one server switches first and the rest follow once it works.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: a canary, where one server only does a change and sees everything working fine and then only moves to others.

statement: The teacher probes: why upload to a new S3 path at all - would uploading to the same path not simplify the solution, since a new path forces telling API servers to update their configuration?
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Why do you want to upload it to a new S3 path? What would happen if you upload to the same path?

statement: Student answer on same-path upload: there may be a short window where the file cannot be served while it uploads, and any deployment needs a rollback plan - if the upload fails or the file gets corrupted, monitoring must detect it and you revert to the previous file.
detail: The teacher thanks the student and later (01:24:27) folds upload failure and corruption into the list of same-path problems.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: when you think about a deployment, you need to think about the rollback part.

statement: Student's addition: put the file in temporary storage first, check it works, and only then mark it successful, so a failed transfer can be rolled back to the previous file.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: having a temporary storage where you put this file and then upload it, check it, it is working fine and then, then mark it successful.

statement: Drawing boxes is easy; the interesting part is the details - where and how to upload, what challenges you would encounter, whether the transition is smooth, whether users are served garbage data. These details are super critical.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: as I said, drawing boxes is easy. When you go into these details, this is where things become really interesting.

statement: The problem statement looks simple (even 'stupid') but after an hour and a half it still has not converged; the problems and solutions here are building blocks that apply to other systems you design.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: these are all building blocks you can apply to other systems that you are designed.

statement: Uploading the new dictionary to the same S3 path has several problems: the upload may fail, the file may get corrupted, and the API servers must be told to reload their index because the offsets no longer match.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So uploading to the same path on S3 had a lot of problems. First, what if upload fails? What if there is file corruption?

statement: Each API server, on its first call to S3, loads the index into memory; every request is then served from the index: check the offset, go to that location, read the meaning and send it back.
case_study: Word dictionary on S3: applying the weekly Oxford changelog to the one-file dictionary served by the API servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: index is loaded in memory on the API server, right? First made call to S3, loaded the index already.

statement: Example: the in-memory index says apple is at offset 100 with 1024 bytes. After a new file is uploaded to the same path, a query for apple reads 1024 bytes at offset 100, which may be some other word (e.g. the one before apple), even starting in the middle - the user sees garbage, because apple's real offset in the new file is different.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now if someone queries Apple, it will go to byte offset 100 and read 1024 bytes, which might be some other random word

statement: With a same-path upload you must immediately tell the API servers to reload their index, and for that duration users see garbage data - a very poor user experience.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you have to immediately tell API servers to reload their index. But for that duration, your users will see garbage data.

statement: So upload to a new path instead, versioning the file name: e.g. s3://word-dictionary/dictionary1.dict first, then s3://word-dictionary/dictionary2.dict for the update. The open question becomes how to tell the API servers to start serving the new path.
case_study: Word dictionary on S3: applying the weekly Oxford changelog to the one-file dictionary served by the API servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now how do you tell API servers that this is the new path you should start serving? How do you communicate this?

statement: Putting something else (e.g. an IP address) in the path changes nothing: whatever the path is, the new path still has to be conveyed to the API servers so they reload.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You have to convey this path, whatever path is, you have to convey this to the API server that this is the new path

statement: A student proposes sending an interrupt or command to every API server to invalidate its cache; the teacher calls pinging all API servers too complex.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Like for ping all API servers to invalidate the cache. Sounds too complex. Isn't it?

statement: A student proposes switching at a known time, since the job's schedule is known; the teacher calls it unreliable: with a cron-style 'Sunday 1 PM, everyone update', the job may run past 1 PM, the upload may fail, or the file may be corrupt and unvalidated, yet the independent trigger would switch anyway.
detail: The student argued the only harm is added latency since servers would go to S3; the teacher: "What if your upload failed completely? What if your file was corrupt?"
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Because if you do a cron job, no matter what, Sunday at 1 PM, everyone update. What if your job ran beyond 1 PM?

statement: A student proposes storing each word in its own file; the teacher rejects it because it kills portability, the constraint the design is playing with.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: No, we, then we kill portability. That's why we are not having each word in one file.

statement: A student proposes a metadata file on S3 holding the current dictionary/index path: after the new file is uploaded (in the PUT request's success callback) the metadata is updated, and API servers poll it every 5-10 minutes and, when the path changes, fetch the new file and rebuild their in-memory index.
case_study: Word dictionary on S3: applying the weekly Oxford changelog to the one-file dictionary served by the API servers.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: we can have some extra file which will have like a metadata.

statement: The metadata file's path must be static (not versioned) so that everyone knows it is the only place to look.
detail: Teacher: "Perfect. Okay. So that everyone knows that this is the only path where we have to go."
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So the path of the metadata file will always be static.

statement: Why poll every 5-10 minutes when the job runs weekly? The student's answer: the exact upload time is unknown - e.g. updates arrive Sunday but S3 is down and the upload happens Monday - so servers poll continuously to find out.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Why would you do that, given that your job runs weekly?

statement: Wherever there is polling, things can be made reactive: instead of polling, someone tells you 'something has changed, go pull' (studied in the second and third weeks).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we can make things wherever we have poll, we can make things reactive.

statement: Reactive option: all API servers subscribe to a Redis Pub/Sub channel, and the update server pushes an event into it when it is done uploading, so every server receives the update.
case_study: Word dictionary on S3: applying the weekly Oxford changelog to the one-file dictionary served by the API servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: All API servers subscribe to Redis Pub/Sub and the new server

statement: With an update once a week, polling 5,000 times before it is unnecessary; reactive avoids it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So your update is happening once every week. Why would you poll 5,000 times before that? Unnecessary.

statement: Redis Pub/Sub seems too complex here: another infrastructure component to run, with every API server listening on persistent connections just to learn that something changed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But this seems too complex having another infrastructure component running and every API server is listening to this.

statement: A student proposes a 'latest' flag (0/1) in the file header, setting the old file's flag to 0 when a new one is uploaded; the teacher says you would never know which file is the latest, and the student concedes it still requires API servers to poll.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: And how would you know the latest one? You would never know it's the latest one or not.

statement: A student proposes keeping the header version with the index and, on each incoming request, checking with the backend whether the version changed; the teacher: you cannot know something changed unless you poll, so it is still polling.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: But how would you know that something changed unless you poll it?
flags: check: speaker of "But you're still polling for that." (Teacher?)

statement: Polling is not bad - the teacher is not against it - but why make 5,000 requests when someone can tell you, or trigger something, instead.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Because polling is good. I'm not against polling. It's just that why to waste, but like why to make 5,000 requests

statement: Exposing a REST endpoint on the API servers that the update server calls is the same reactive approach as Pub/Sub.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You expose a REST endpoint and this server calls that.

statement: A student proposes upgrading one API server at a time: servers register with the update job, it sends each an event to rebuild its index from the new path, tests it, then tells the load balancer (e.g. via a new port); the teacher calls it complex - the same thing can be done in a very simple way.
detail: The teacher also notes the path is already in meta.json, so there is no need to tell it to the server; the API servers loading the index is a normal stage.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: You are trying to change port of the servers and this and that. This can be done in a very simple way.
flags: check: "complex" repeated 6x in ASR; may be the teacher interrupting

statement: Make the solution utterly simple, something anyone would be able to understand: that is where the beauty of system design lies.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I'm just trying to make it utter simple, like something that anyone would be able to understand.

statement: meta.json is a static file containing the path of the dictionary to serve. When an API server boots it reads meta.json, sees the path, reads the dictionary, builds the index and starts serving.
case_study: Word dictionary on S3: applying the weekly Oxford changelog to the one-file dictionary served by the API servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: given that we now have a static file, meta.json, which contains the path of the dictionary that needs to be served

statement: Hint: after the path in meta.json is updated, what is needed is to trigger a reload of the API servers, which is literally what happens on boot.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So what you're doing is when you're updating this and updating this path, you have to trigger a reload of this API server.

statement: A student proposes uploading to the same path with S3 versioning enabled; the teacher says that is going S3-specific and is exactly what creating two separate files already does.
detail: Teacher at 01:40:44: different files plus a meta file that says which one is active = the latest version; internally S3 can abstract it out, but it is laid out here in very simple terms.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Like that's exactly what we did with creating two files separate.

statement: A student proposes adding an updated_at attribute to meta.json and checking it on every request; the teacher: that is still polling, and a call to the meta.json file on every request is expensive.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: But on every request made, making a meta call to meta JSON file, expensive.

statement: A student proposes checking an updated_at/created_at value of the dictionary file itself before each read; the teacher rejects it: reading with the old index gives garbage data, forcing another read and an index reload, and a text file does not store such metadata at its top.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: No, for the text file, for the text file, no, that are not stored there.

statement: Reloading the API servers after meta.json is updated is equivalent to doing a deployment: a rebooted server reads meta.json, goes to the path, reads the file and index, builds the hash map and starts serving requests.
case_study: Word dictionary on S3: applying the weekly Oxford changelog to the one-file dictionary served by the API servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we just want to trigger a server reload, which is equivalent to doing a deployment.

statement: The update job includes the AWS SDK and triggers a deployment through the deployment pipeline; with rolling deployment configured it takes down one server and spins up another, and the new machine reads the metadata file on boot, gets the new path, reads it and serves it.
case_study: Word dictionary on S3: applying the weekly Oxford changelog to the one-file dictionary served by the API servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You just include your AWS SDK and trigger a deployment using a deployment pipeline

statement: During the rolling deployment there is inconsistency - some requests hit servers with the index on the old data, others hit new servers with the new data - but no garbage is served; the data is eventually consistent, which is fine because meanings do not change drastically.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You are serving eventually consistent data, but that's fine because meanings anyway does not change drastically.

statement: Any deployment strategy is fine; trigger the deployment with whatever you use (cloud provider, Jenkins job) - one deployment invocation replaces API endpoints, reactive Pub/Sub and all of that.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: instead of exposing API endpoints, reactive, Redis Pub/Sub, all of that, throw it out of the window. Trigger a simple deployment

statement: The teacher's pre-written notes cover the same flow in more detail: changelog, merge, uploading to the same path, transition, reactive Pub/Sub, parallel setup (what was just done), and portability by adding a header.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Changelog, how it would happen, merge that we just discussed, uploading it to the same path, transition, reactive Pub/Sub, parallel setup.

statement: What the design achieves: seamless pointed GET requests on S3 (not PUT) that read only the bare minimum amount of data needed; this has huge applications.
case_study: Word dictionary on S3: applying the weekly Oxford changelog to the one-file dictionary served by the API servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Pointed reads, reading the bare minimum amount of data that you have to. This has huge applications.

statement: Amazon orders: users are highly unlikely to access orders made six months back, so push orders older than six months to S3; recent orders are served from the hot database (e.g. MySQL) and old ones read from S3, since users can still go back and check them.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Amazon orders, how likely are you to access orders that you made six months back? Highly unlikely, right?

statement: You cannot just dump everything on S3 in a JSON file; you need the ability to make pointed queries on S3 (e.g. order ID -> order details), which is what this dictionary design gives.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: On S3, you cannot just dump everything in a JSON file. You need an ability to make pointed queries on S3.

statement: This simple word-dictionary-on-S3 system lays the foundation for multi-tiered storage, because the data dumped on S3 does not lose the ability to be queried.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it lays the foundation for multi-tiered storages, because we are not losing an ability to query the data that we dump on S3.

statement: S3 here is not archival but cheap storage: keeping very infrequently accessed data on S3 trades off time (hot database fast, S3 relatively very slow) for a significant reduction in the cost of the hot database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In most places, you think that, hey, when I dump on S3, it's archival. Here, it's a cheap storage for us.

statement: Athena does exactly this: you can load a CSV file and fire queries on it; behind the scenes it creates an index kept handy with the file, and on a request goes to the file, reads the records and serves them.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Athena does exactly this. On Athena, you can load a CSV file and fire queries on this.

statement: What was built is the ability to fire a simple get-key request on S3 without reading the entire file - a simple key-value format to start with, more complex later.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: to fire a simple get key request on S3 without, without having to read this entire file. We just built it.

statement: Data lakes store huge amounts of data in very cheap storage while keeping the ability to query it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: data lakes are where you're storing huge amount of data in a very cheap storage, but having an ability to query it.

statement: Apache Hudi does exactly this behind the scenes - the Hudi table format is exactly this kind of stored index - and Hive partitions are exactly this too; it is the foundation for querying huge data on very cheap storage.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Apache Hudi does exactly this behind the scenes. The format that Hudi table format is exactly this index that we are storing.

statement: Summary of the word dictionary on S3: from deciding to development to deployment and seamless transitions, keep things really simple rather than over-complicated.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: seamless transitions and everything, and keeping things really simple rather than over complicated.

statement: Order of steps in the update job: create the merged file, upload it to a new S3 path, update meta.json with that path, and only then trigger the deployment of the API servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So in that new server, when this meta.json file is updated, we are just triggering a deployment of our API servers.
flags: check: "Yes. Yes." may be the teacher confirming

statement: A student asks whether something better than a whole redeployment (new VM) is possible, since only the startup process - read meta, build index, serve - needs to rerun; the teacher can imagine three ways, e.g. API endpoints that trigger a reload of the API servers (reactive), but they make things a little more complicated.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: I can imagine three ways to do it, but it's just, just make things little more complicated.

statement: Triggering a deployment as the API-server reload is an out-of-the-box approach many engineers do not think about: the cost stays the same, but you avoid polling the metadata file and reactive Pub/Sub; we control our own infrastructure and can use it to get things done.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Thinking of triggering a deployment as part of an API server reload is an out of the box approach

statement: Another alternative: instead of API servers reading the index from S3, send the actual index data in the update sent to them - it is just 1.7 MB - so no reload is needed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What if in the updates that we are sending to API servers, what if we send the actual index data? It's just 1.7 MB, right?

statement: After the break: building a super fast database (key-value store) that everyone uses unknowingly, with O(1) reads, writes and deletes plus persistence, going deeper into what the file format should be (not simple CSVs) to get max performance out of the hard disk.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we'll make order one reads, order one writes, order one deletes with persistence.
